specPoints.text: understand experiments that can be used to investigate reaction rates by: i an initial-rate method, carrying out separate experiments where different initial concentrations of one reagent are used A ‘clock reaction’ is an acceptable approximation of this method. ii a continuous monitoring method to generate data to enable concentration-time or volume-time graphs to be plotted

primer.text: Continuous monitoring collects concentration data throughout a reaction rather than at a single moment. This note walks the iodination of propanone followed by colorimetry: building a calibration curve from standard iodine solutions, mixing measured volumes, logging absorbance against time, and reading the rate at any instant as the gradient of a tangent.

lessons.title: Watching the whole reaction: colorimetric monitoring
lessons.opening: Continuous monitoring collects data across the entire reaction instead of one moment. The showcase is iodine's decolourisation during propanone iodination in acid: a calibration curve converts colorimeter absorbance into iodine concentration, and the logged readings trace the whole concentration-time curve.
keyPoints: Continuous monitoring collects experimental data throughout the reaction so a full concentration-time graph can be plotted.
In the iodination of propanone, catalysed by dilute sulfuric acid, brown iodine decolourises as it forms iodopropanone and hydrogen iodide.
A colorimeter reads absorbance, and absorbance scales with how concentrated the coloured species is.
Before the run, absorbances of standard iodine solutions are measured to build a calibration curve for converting readings into concentrations.
Four burettes hold 0.02 mol dm-3 iodine, 1.0 mol dm-3 propanone, 1.0 mol dm-3 sulfuric acid and distilled water, so volumes can be varied while the total stays constant.

low.restatement: Calibrate first with standard iodine solutions, mix measured volumes, start the timer as iodine joins, and log absorbance throughout.
low.analogy: Fitting a backstage translator (the calibration curve) before the show, so every applause meter reading (absorbance) converts into audience numbers (concentration).
low.examPointer: Name the calibration curve's job explicitly: absorbance in, concentration out.

medium.restatement: Because iodine is the only strongly coloured species, its absorbance is a live read-out of [I2]; the calibration curve anchors the scale so numbers, not just shapes, come out.
medium.analogy: A fuel gauge calibrated before the drive: the needle's position only means something once you know what empty and full are.
medium.examPointer: The iodine beaker is added last because adding it starts the reaction - mixing order is timing order.

check.stem: In the iodination of propanone, the role of dilute sulfuric acid is

options.explanation: The acid catalyses while iodine decolourises.

The colorimeter provides the signal.

check.stem: The calibration curve is needed before the experiment because

options.text: Absorbance readings must be convertible into iodine concentrations
options.explanation: The curve maps absorbance to concentration for the species being followed.
Cleaning is not the curve's purpose.
Calibration does not touch kinetics.
Iodine's colour is exactly what is measured.

check.stem: Four burettes are used with distilled water maintaining constant total volume so that

options.text: Concentrations can be varied between runs while keeping the mixture volume fixed
options.explanation: Volume control isolates concentration as the changed variable.

options.text: The colorimeter can hold four samples
options.explanation: One cuvette is read at a time.
Colour is not the design reason.
Speed is not the goal of the volume design.

options.text: Adding the iodine starts the reaction, so it must join the other liquids as the stopwatch starts
options.explanation: Mixing order and clock order are the same order.
Evaporation is not the stated reason.
Iodine is precisely what it reads.
No such incompatibility exists.

check.stem: State the equation for the acid-catalysed iodination of propanone.
check.modelAnswer: CH3COCH3 + I2 gives CH3COCH2I and HI, with dilute sulfuric acid as catalyst.

check.stem: State what is measured before the investigation begins.
check.modelAnswer: The absorbances of a set of standard iodine solutions, to obtain the calibration curve.

check.stem: Explain why absorbance can track iodine concentration during the run.
check.modelAnswer: Iodine is the coloured species being consumed, and absorbance is proportional to a coloured species' concentration, so each logged reading gives the iodine concentration at that instant once the calibration curve is applied.

check.stem: A student mixes propanone and acid, then adds iodine fifteen seconds before starting the data logger. Comment on the consequence.
check.modelAnswer: The reaction ran unlogged for fifteen seconds, so the earliest data are missing; the curve still exists but its opening section must be extrapolated, and the missing window weakens any early-gradient reading.

lessons.title: Volumes, results and rates at any instant
sourceHeadings: Specimen Results Table for the Iodination of Propanone
lessons.opening: The specimen tables show the run's design and its output: volume recipes for each mixture, then logged iodine concentrations against time. A tangent at any chosen moment converts the curve into an instantaneous rate, demonstrated at 300 seconds.
keyPoints: The volume compositions table lists burette volumes for each run, with distilled water keeping the total constant.
The specimen results table and its graph record iodine concentration falling through the reaction.
A practical tip: choose the filter giving the strongest absorbance, the complementary colour to the solution's own.
The rate at any point comes from drawing a tangent and finding its gradient.
At 300 seconds the tangent's gradient is 0.0069/590 = 1.17 x 10^-5 mol dm-3 s^-1.

low.restatement: The results table feeds the concentration-time curve; a tangent at any chosen time gives that instant's rate by gradient.
low.analogy: A marathon split chart: pick any checkpoint, measure the local pace, and that pace is the rate at that moment.
low.examPointer: For tangent marks, quote the rise and the run, then the units mol dm-3 s^-1.

medium.restatement: Continuous data let you interrogate any instant, which is exactly what order analysis needs: gradients at several times reveal how rate responds to the falling concentration.
medium.analogy: A flight recorder: rather than one number for the whole journey, every moment is recoverable.
medium.examPointer: The complementary-colour filter rule earns marks in practical-write-up questions.

options.text: The burette volumes of iodine, propanone, acid and water for each run
options.explanation: The recipes let concentration be varied at fixed total volume.
Absorbance lives in the results table.
Temperature is not the table's content.
The catalyst is fixed, not tabulated per run.

check.stem: The practical tip for filter choice says to pick the filter that

options.text: Gives the strongest absorbance, the complementary colour to the solution
options.explanation: Strong absorbance maximises the signal.
A weak signal drowns in noise.
Complementary, not matching, is the rule.
Cost is not the criterion.

check.stem: The rate at 300 seconds is found by

options.text: Drawing a vertical line to the curve at 300 s, adding a tangent, and taking its gradient
options.explanation: The local gradient is the local rate.
That is an average, not an instantaneous rate.

options.text: Reading the concentration at 300 s directly
options.explanation: Concentration is not rate.
No such operation exists.

check.stem: The tangent at 300 seconds on the specimen graph gives a rate of

options.explanation: The rise over run computes to about 1.17e-5.
The quotient is inverted.
That is the rise, not the gradient.
The power of ten is wildly off.

check.stem: Watching iodine concentration continuously earns its keep in order analysis because

options.text: Gradients at many times show how rate responds to changing concentration
options.explanation: Multiple tangents expose the rate-concentration relationship.
It needs a colorimeter and data logger.

options.text: Each run gives only one rate
options.explanation: It gives rates at every instant.
The falling concentration is the whole point.

check.stem: State the gradient calculation demonstrated at 300 seconds.
check.modelAnswer: 0.0069 divided by 590, giving 1.17 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3 s^-1.

check.stem: State what the specimen results table and its graph record.
check.modelAnswer: The iodine concentration falling as the reaction proceeds, against time.

check.stem: Explain why a tangent, rather than a chord, is used to read the rate at 300 seconds.
check.modelAnswer: A chord averages the rate over an interval, while a tangent touches the curve at one instant, so only the tangent's gradient is the instantaneous rate at exactly 300 seconds.

check.stem: Two tangents on the same results curve give 1.17 x 10^-5 at 300 s and a smaller value at 600 s. What does the shrinkage suggest about the order in iodine?
check.modelAnswer: The rate falls as iodine concentration falls, so the rate depends on iodine concentration - behaviour pointing to a positive order in iodine rather than zero order.

glossary.definition: Collecting concentration data throughout a reaction to plot a full concentration-time graph.
A plot of absorbance against concentration for standard solutions, used to convert readings into concentrations.
The small receptacle holding the sample inside the colorimeter.

workedExample.prompt: On the specimen results graph, draw a vertical line from the 300 s mark up to the curve and add the tangent there. The tangent falls 0.0069 units over a run of 590 units. Find the rate of reaction at 300 seconds.
steps: Apply the gradient formula to the tangent: rise divided by run.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The rate at 300 s is 1.17 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3 s^-1.
